title: CI/CD Foundations & Git workflow
scopeHtml:
Scope: CI vs continuous delivery vs deployment, why small batches win, branching strategies, pull-request gates and environment promotion.

Scope: commit conventions, versioning, monorepos, DevOps and platform engineering, release trains.

notes.title: What CI, CD and Continuous Deployment mean
notes.html:
Continuous Integration (CI) means every developer merges small changes into the shared branch often (at least daily), and a machine automatically builds and tests each change. Continuous Delivery (CD) means every change that passes is ready to ship at the push of a button. Continuous Deployment goes one step further: every passing change ships to production automatically, with no human click.

The three terms differ only in the last arrow. Delivery = a human presses the button. Deployment = a machine does.

Worked example. A team of 20 merges ~40 PRs a day. Without CI they find out two weeks later that PR 7 and PR 31 break each other. With CI the second PR fails its build within 8 minutes, while the author still remembers the code.

Industry examples. Amazon deploys to production roughly every few seconds across its services; Netflix, Etsy and Google do thousands of deploys per day. Banks usually do Continuous Delivery with a manual approval, because of audit rules.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant kitchen where every dish is tasted at each station (CI). Delivery means the dish sits on the pass ready for the waiter to take; deployment means a conveyor belt carries it to the table by itself.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "CD" without saying which one. Always ask or state: delivery or deployment.
  • Thinking CI means "we use Jenkins". CI is a practice (merge often, test every merge); the tool is incidental.
  • Calling a nightly build "CI". Nightly is not continuous.

notes.title: Why teams do it (the problems it removes)
notes.html:
Before CI, teams had integration hell (big-bang merges), works on my machine bugs, manual release checklists run at 2 a.m., and fear of releasing so releases became rare and huge. Huge releases are riskier, so teams released even less: a vicious circle.

The fix is small batches. Smaller changes are easier to test, easier to review, easier to roll back, and when one breaks you know which commit caused it.

The DORA metrics (from Google's DevOps Research) measure this: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and time to restore service. Elite teams deploy on demand, have lead time under a day, failure rate under ~15%, and recover in under an hour.

Industry examples. GitHub deploys its monolith many times a day using feature flags; Facebook ships its web code to production at least daily; Spotify squads own their own pipelines.

Everyday analogy. Moving house: ten small trips with a car are safer than one giant truck trip that, if it breaks down, strands everything.

Common interview traps.

  • "CI/CD makes software faster to write." It makes delivery safer and faster, not coding.
  • Forgetting the cultural half: CI only works if people keep the main branch green and fix a broken build immediately.

notes.title: Branching strategies: trunk-based vs GitFlow
notes.html:
Trunk-based development: everyone commits to main (or very short-lived branches, under a day or two). Unfinished work is hidden behind feature flags. This is what CI/CD is designed for.

GitFlow: long-lived develop, release/*, hotfix/* branches. Good for versioned products shipped on a schedule (mobile apps, on-prem software), but slow merges and big diffs fight against continuous integration.

GitHub Flow: a middle path. main is always deployable; short feature branch, PR, review, merge, deploy.

Trunk-based:   main ──●──●──●──●──●──●──►   (short branches, flags)
GitFlow:       main ──────────●─────────●─►
               develop ─●──●──●──●──●──●─►
               feature/x  ╲__●__●__╱   (lives for days or weeks)

Worked example. A 3-week feature branch touches 60 files; by merge day main has moved 120 commits and the merge takes two days. The same feature behind a flag, merged in 12 small PRs, never has a conflict bigger than 10 lines.

Industry examples. Google and Meta run enormous monorepos on trunk-based development. Android and many enterprise products still use release branches because shipped versions must be patched.

Everyday analogy. A shared Google Doc everyone edits live (trunk) versus emailing Word files around and merging by hand later (long branches).

Common interview traps.

  • Declaring one strategy "best". The honest answer ties it to release model: continuous web service → trunk; versioned, multi-supported product → release branches.
  • Forgetting feature flags are the prerequisite for trunk-based work.

notes.title: Pull requests as the quality gate
notes.html:
A pull request (PR) is where CI meets humans. The pipeline runs on the PR: build, unit tests, lint, security scan. Branch protection (a repo setting) blocks merging until required checks are green and N reviewers approve. A merge queue serialises merges and re-tests each PR on top of the latest main, so two individually green PRs cannot combine into a red main.

Good PR hygiene: small (under ~400 changed lines), one purpose, description with how to test, linked ticket.

Worked example. Two PRs each pass alone. PR A renames getUser to fetchUser; PR B adds a new call to getUser. Merging both breaks main. A merge queue tests B on top of A and rejects it before it lands.

Industry examples. GitHub Merge Queue, GitLab Merge Trains, Bors, and Shopify's and Uber's custom merge queues exist exactly for this.

Everyday analogy. A checkout lane at a store: each cart is scanned and bagged in order, so one person's items never mix into another's.

Common interview traps.

  • Requiring checks but allowing admins to bypass them "just this once": this is how outages start.
  • Flaky tests: a test that fails randomly trains people to click "re-run" and ignore red. Quarantine and fix them.

notes.title: Environments and promotion
notes.html:
Code moves through environments: dev (developer sandbox) → test/QA → staging (production-like) → production. The key rule is build once, deploy many: the same artifact (the same Docker image digest) is promoted through every environment; only configuration changes. Rebuilding per environment means you tested something different from what you ship.

Configuration (URLs, secrets, flags) lives outside the artifact: environment variables, a config service, or a secrets manager. This follows the Twelve-Factor App rules.

Industry examples. Netflix Spinnaker promotes one baked image through test and prod stages; Amazon's Apollo/Pipelines do the same.

Everyday analogy. A product leaves the factory once, sealed in its box; different countries get the same box with a different plug adapter.

Common interview traps.

  • Recompiling in each environment ("it worked in staging but prod got a different build").
  • Putting secrets in the image or in git.

notes.title: Commit hygiene and conventional commits
notes.html:
A pipeline is only as useful as the history it runs on. Good habits: small, single-purpose commits; a message that says why, not just what; no secrets, no generated files. Conventional Commits (feat:, fix:, chore:, feat!: for breaking) give commits a machine-readable shape, so tools can pick the next version number and write the changelog automatically (semantic-release, release-please).

feat(cart): allow coupon stacking
fix(auth): refresh token before expiry
feat!: drop v1 API   <- "!" means breaking change -> major version bump

Pre-commit hooks (Husky, pre-commit) run formatters and linters locally for instant feedback; CI repeats them because hooks can be skipped.

Industry examples. Angular popularised the commit convention; Google's Chromium and Linux require signed-off, descriptive commits; many SaaS repos auto-release on merge using these prefixes.

Everyday analogy. A well-kept lab notebook: dated, specific entries let anyone retrace what was done and why.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing a local hook replaces CI. Hooks are advisory; CI is the enforcement point.
  • Giant "fix stuff" commits that cannot be reverted cleanly.

notes.title: Versioning and release tagging
notes.html:
Semantic Versioning (SemVer): MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Patch = bug fix, minor = backwards-compatible feature, major = breaking change. A git tag (v2.4.1) marks exactly which commit was released; the pipeline can trigger a release when a tag is pushed. CalVer (2025.11.3) suits apps released on a calendar.

Every artifact should carry its identity: the image tag has the commit SHA; the build embeds the version and SHA (visible at /version or in logs) so on-call can answer "what is running?" in seconds.

Worked example. Library at 2.3.4. Fix a null pointer → 2.3.5. Add a new optional method → 2.4.0. Remove a method → 3.0.0, and consumers know to read the migration notes.

Industry examples. npm, Maven Central and Go modules rely on SemVer; Ubuntu uses CalVer (24.04); Chrome ships numbered releases on a fixed train.

Everyday analogy. Edition numbers of a textbook: a corrected typo, a new chapter, and a complete rewrite are different kinds of change.

Common interview traps.

  • Shipping a breaking change in a minor version.
  • Moving a tag to a different commit. Tags should be immutable.

notes.title: Monorepo vs polyrepo and what it does to CI
notes.html:
Monorepo: many services in one repository (Google, Meta, Uber). Easy atomic cross-service changes and shared tooling, but CI must be smart: run only what a change affects, using path filters or build tools (Bazel, Nx, Turborepo, Gradle) that know the dependency graph. Polyrepo: one repository per service; clean ownership and simple per-repo pipelines, but cross-repo changes are painful and versions drift.

monorepo change: libs/auth/**  ->  rebuild + test: auth, api, checkout (dependents only)
                                    skip: search, notifications

Worked example. A monorepo with 60 services and a 40-minute full test run is unusable on every PR. With affected-only testing, a typical PR runs 3 services in 6 minutes.

Industry examples. Google (Piper, Blaze/Bazel) and Meta (Buck) built custom systems; many startups use Nx or Turborepo with remote caches.

Everyday analogy. One big shared kitchen (needs rules so you only wash your own dishes) versus separate kitchens in each flat.

Common interview traps.

  • Running the whole test suite for every change in a monorepo.
  • Polyrepo with copy-pasted pipelines that diverge; fix with shared templates.

notes.title: DevOps culture and platform engineering
notes.html:
DevOps is not a job title or a tool; it is a way of working: developers and operations share responsibility for running software ("you build it, you run it"), automate the path to production, and learn from failures without blame. Typical practices: infrastructure as code, CI/CD, monitoring, on-call by the owning team, blameless post-mortems.

Platform engineering is the next step: a small team builds an internal developer platform (golden-path pipeline templates, deployment tooling, service catalogue such as Backstage) so product teams self-serve without learning every tool. The platform is treated as a product, with developers as its customers.

Worked example. Creating a new service used to take two weeks of tickets. A platform template creates the repo, pipeline, Kubernetes manifests, dashboards and alerts in 20 minutes.

Industry examples. Spotify created Backstage; Netflix has a "paved road"; Amazon's "two-pizza teams own their service end to end".

Everyday analogy. Instead of every family building its own road to town, the city builds a highway and gives each family an on-ramp.

Common interview traps.

  • Defining DevOps as "the person who manages Jenkins".
  • A platform team that mandates tools without listening to users, so teams work around it.

notes.title: Release trains and versioned products
notes.html:
Not everything is a web service. Mobile apps, desktop software and on-prem products cannot be rolled back by redeploying: users hold old versions. They use release trains (a fixed cadence, e.g. every two weeks; whatever is ready ships), release branches for stabilisation, hotfix branches for old versions, and staged rollouts (1% → 100%) in the store.

CI still applies: every commit builds and tests; the release branch gets extra regression testing; signing keys live in a secrets store; the pipeline uploads to the store track (internal → beta → production).

Worked example. Android app on a 2-week train: branch cut on Monday, beta to 5% on Wednesday, production at 10% on Friday, 50% the next Monday if crash-free sessions stay above 99.5%.

Industry examples. Chrome (4-week cadence), WhatsApp and Instagram use staged store rollouts, force-update screens and server-side flags to disable broken features without a new build.

Everyday analogy. A bus timetable: the bus leaves on schedule with whoever is ready, instead of waiting for every passenger.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming you can "just redeploy" a mobile fix; store review and user update lag make server-side flags essential.
  • Delaying a train for one feature; the next train is only two weeks away.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html: CI = merge small changes often and test each automatically; Continuous Delivery = always releasable; Continuous Deployment = releases automatically. The point is small batches, which are safer and faster. Prefer trunk-based development with feature flags for services; keep release branches only when versions must be maintained. Protect main with required checks, reviews and a merge queue, keep tests non-flaky, build the artifact once and promote it through environments with only the configuration changing. Measure yourself with the four DORA metrics.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between Continuous Integration, Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates who use the words loosely usually have not owned a release process.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: CI is merging small changes often and having a machine build and test every one. Continuous Delivery means every passing change is ready to release at the push of a button. Continuous Deployment removes the button: every passing change goes to production automatically.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: All three share the same pipeline; they differ in how far it runs automatically. CI covers commit → build → test. Delivery adds packaging and deployment to a production-like environment, with a human decision before production. Deployment adds the automatic production step. Regulated businesses (banks) usually stop at delivery because of approval and audit rules.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "CD" without saying which one.
  • Equating CI with a tool (Jenkins) instead of a practice (merge daily, test every merge).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which would you choose for a payments service? → Delivery with an automated pipeline and an approval gate; deployment for low-risk internal tools.
  2. What must exist before Continuous Deployment is safe? → Fast reliable tests, feature flags, monitoring with automatic rollback.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE defines the terms. Senior ties the choice to risk, audit needs and rollback ability.

questions.promptHtml: Why do small, frequent releases reduce risk instead of increasing it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand the core idea (small batches) rather than the tooling.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A small change is easy to review, easy to test, and when it breaks you know exactly which commit did it, so rollback is quick. A huge release mixes hundreds of changes, so failures are hard to find and fix, which makes people release even less often.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Risk grows faster than linearly with batch size because changes interact. Frequent releases also keep the release process practiced and automated. The DORA research found elite teams are both faster and more stable: speed and stability are not a trade-off. The four metrics are deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying CI/CD speeds up coding; it speeds up safe delivery.
  • Quoting the metrics without being able to explain how to improve one.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Your lead time is 9 days; where do you look first? → Usually waiting time (review queues, release windows), not CI duration.
  2. Which metric measures stability? → Change failure rate and time to restore.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior points out that most lead time is queueing, and ties it to batch size.

questions.promptHtml: Compare trunk-based development with GitFlow. When would you pick each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows if you can match a workflow to a release model.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Trunk-based means tiny branches merged to main within a day or two, with unfinished work hidden behind feature flags; it fits services deployed continuously. GitFlow uses long-lived develop and release branches and fits versioned products that must be patched for years, like on-prem software or some mobile releases.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Long-lived branches delay integration, so conflicts grow and tests run on code that is not what ships. Trunk-based development needs flags, strong automated tests and a green main. GitFlow gives isolation and release stabilisation at the cost of merge pain and slower feedback. GitHub Flow is a middle path: short feature branch, PR, deploy from main.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Declaring one "best" regardless of context.
  • Trunk-based without feature flags, so half-built features reach users.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you ship an unfinished feature on trunk? → Behind a feature flag defaulting off.
  2. How do you patch an old version in trunk-based? → Cherry-pick the fix to a short-lived release branch.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior connects the strategy to the deployment frequency and the number of supported versions.

questions.promptHtml: Two pull requests each pass CI, but main breaks after both merge. How do you prevent this?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests knowledge of semantic merge conflicts and merge queues.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each PR was tested against an older main, so combined they can fail even without textual conflicts. A merge queue (GitHub Merge Queue, GitLab Merge Trains, Bors) tests each PR on top of the latest main plus the PRs ahead of it, and only merges if green.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Alternative is "require branches to be up to date" before merge, but then every merge forces everyone else to rebase and re-run CI. A queue batches and serialises this automatically. Pair it with branch protection (required checks, reviews, no admin bypass).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Letting admins bypass required checks "just this once".
  • Ignoring flaky tests, which make queues retry constantly.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does the queue cost? → Extra CI capacity and slightly longer time to merge.
  2. How do flaky tests affect it? → They eject good PRs; quarantine and fix them.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior mentions the cost trade-off and batching.

questions.promptHtml: What does "build once, deploy many" mean and why does it matter?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks understanding of artifact promotion and reproducibility.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: You build the artifact (for example a Docker image) one time, identify it by digest or commit SHA, and promote that exact artifact through dev, staging and production. Only configuration changes between environments. If you rebuilt per environment, what you tested would not be what you ship.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: A rebuild can pull different dependency versions or a different base image. Configuration (URLs, secrets, flags) comes from environment variables, a config service or a secrets manager, per the Twelve-Factor App. Promotion means moving the same tag or digest forward after the previous stage's tests pass.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Baking environment-specific config or secrets into the image.
  • Deploying latest so you cannot say what is running.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you roll back? → Redeploy the previous immutable digest.
  2. Where do secrets live? → A secrets manager or encrypted store, injected at runtime.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior includes provenance and signing so you can prove the artifact is the one that was tested.

questions.contextHtml: A 25-engineer team has long-lived feature branches (average 9 days), merges take 1-2 days of conflict fixing, and the CI pipeline takes 45 minutes. Releases happen every 3 weeks and about 1 in 4 causes a rollback.
questions.promptHtml: How would you improve the delivery process over the next quarter?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Buy faster CI machines and add more tests." This ignores batch size and branching.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Where does lead time go (waiting vs CI)? How flaky are the tests? Are there multiple supported versions? What are the compliance constraints?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Measure DORA metrics and break the lead time down; quarantine flaky tests.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Long branches cause merge pain; 45-minute CI discourages small PRs; manual release steps add risk.
  4. How I'd verify: Timestamp PR open, first review, merge, deploy; CI duration by stage.
  5. Root cause: Big batches and slow feedback reinforce each other.
  6. Fix: Move to short-lived branches with feature flags; parallelise and shard CI to under 10 minutes; add a merge queue; automate release to staging; release weekly then daily.
  7. Prevention: Track the four DORA metrics; set a PR size guideline.
  8. Trade-offs: Flags add cleanup work; I would not mandate trunk-based overnight, I would pilot on one team.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Compliance requires manual approval → keep Continuous Delivery with an approval gate, automate everything else.
  • Tests are too slow to fix quickly → run only affected tests on PRs and the full suite post-merge.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team's 3-week release hid a payments bug among 140 changes; it took two days to find. After moving to daily releases the same class of bug was found in under an hour.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tools only, no process change.
  • Hire: smaller batches, faster CI, measured improvement.
  • Strong hire: diagnoses queueing time, stages the change, handles compliance and metrics.

questions.promptHtml: What are Conventional Commits and how do they help automation?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows whether you connect git habits to release automation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A commit message convention such as feat:, fix: and feat!: for breaking changes. Tools like semantic-release or release-please read the prefixes to choose the next version number and generate the changelog automatically.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: fix bumps the patch, feat the minor, a ! or BREAKING CHANGE the major. Pre-commit hooks give instant local feedback, but CI must repeat the checks because hooks can be skipped.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking local hooks replace CI.
  • Giant "misc fixes" commits that cannot be reverted cleanly.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you enforce the format? → A commit-lint check in CI on PR titles or commits.
  2. Squash or keep commits? → Squash-merge with a conventional title keeps history clean.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior ties it to automated releases and traceability.

questions.promptHtml: Explain semantic versioning and why release tags should be immutable.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Version discipline underpins dependency management and rollback.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: patch for bug fixes, minor for backwards-compatible features, major for breaking changes. A git tag marks exactly which commit was released, so moving it would make "what is running?" unanswerable and break reproducibility.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Embed version and commit SHA in the build and expose it (a /version endpoint or log line). CalVer suits calendar-driven apps. Consumers rely on SemVer to decide whether to upgrade safely.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Breaking change in a minor release.
  • Re-pointing a tag to a new commit.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What triggers a release in the pipeline? → Pushing a tag (or merging a release PR).
  2. How do you handle pre-releases? → 1.4.0-rc.1 tags.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior links versions to artifacts, provenance and rollback.

questions.promptHtml: What are the CI implications of a monorepo compared with many repositories?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Large organisations choose one or the other, and pipelines differ a lot.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A monorepo gives atomic cross-service changes and shared tooling, but CI must run only what a change affects, using a dependency graph (Bazel, Nx, Gradle, Turborepo) and remote caches. Polyrepo gives simple per-repo pipelines and clear ownership but makes cross-repo changes and version alignment painful.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Without affected-only testing a monorepo's CI time grows with repo size. Path filters are a rough tool and miss shared-library dependencies; graph-based tools are safer. Run the full suite on main or nightly as a safety net.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Running every test for every PR.
  • Copy-pasted pipelines across polyrepos that drift apart.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you keep required checks working with path filters? → A final gate job that always reports.
  2. Who owns what? → CODEOWNERS per directory.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior discusses build graph, caching and ownership at scale.

questions.promptHtml: What does DevOps mean to you, and what is platform engineering?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates reduce DevOps to tools.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: DevOps is a way of working: teams share responsibility for building and running software, automate the path to production, and learn from failures without blame. Platform engineering builds an internal developer platform with golden-path templates and self-service, so product teams get pipelines, deployments and dashboards without mastering every tool.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The platform is a product with developers as customers; measure adoption and developer satisfaction. Backstage-style catalogs help discovery. The risk is a platform team that dictates tools without feedback.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "DevOps is the person who manages Jenkins."
  • Mandating a platform nobody wants, so teams route around it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you measure a platform? → Time to first deploy, adoption, DORA metrics, developer surveys.
  2. You build it you run it? → The owning team is on call for its service.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior frames it as reducing cognitive load and measures outcomes.

questions.promptHtml: How does releasing a mobile app differ from releasing a web service?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: You cannot roll back installed client apps.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Users hold old versions and store review plus update lag delay fixes, so you use release trains on a fixed cadence, staged store rollouts with crash-free thresholds, server-side feature flags and remote config as kill switches, force-update for dangerously old versions, and keep the backend API backward compatible.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: A release branch is cut for stabilisation, beta goes to a small percentage, and the rollout halts if crash-free sessions drop below a threshold such as 99.5%. Hotfix branches patch old versions that still matter.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming you can "just redeploy" a fix.
  • Delaying a train for one feature.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you disable a crashing feature without a new build? → Remote config or flag.
  2. How long must the API support old clients? → Until usage of the old version falls below an agreed threshold.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior designs the kill-switch and API-compatibility policy.
